result:
The kettle clicked off just as the light outside shifted from gold to that thin blue that means the day is already deciding to leave. I poured the water anyway, watching the steam curl up and vanish against the window. Outside, a single crow sat on the fence post like it had been assigned the job of watching the street. It didn’t move when a car passed. It didn’t move when the neighbor’s dog barked twice and gave up. It just stayed, black against the paling sky, as if waiting for a signal only it could hear.

I thought about how many things in a day are like that crow—present, unbothered, occupying their exact square of the world without explanation. The mug warming my hands. The small crack in the ceiling that has looked the same for three years. The way the radio, left on low in the other room, was playing a song I half-recognized and didn’t need to name. None of these things were asking to be improved or understood. They were simply occurring, and I was occurring alongside them.

It is easy to forget that most of life is not a plot. Most of life is the space between the things we later call events. The waiting. The noticing. The quiet refusal of the crow to be anything other than a crow on a fence at dusk. I drank the tea while it was still too hot, the way I always do, and felt the small burn on my tongue as proof that I was here, in this particular minute, with no better place to be.
